rows.evidence: Q1: Section 2.2 and Fig. 2 report the authors' own SDrOP model runs comparing life cycle cost and irrigation reliability of SSO vs SPM designs for a simulated Kenyan farm; Section 4 reports a seven-day experiment with a prototype controller in Cambridge, MA.
rows.notes: The 18<U+2013>74% lifetime cost saving and 31<U+2013>66% reliability improvement quoted in the passage come entirely from the economic analysis in Section 2.2 (Fig. 2), which is a SDrOP life-cycle-cost optimisation and season simulation run on design data for a hypothetical 2 ha tomato farm in Nyeri, Kenya (Table 1) with three well depths; the simulated cost and reliability outputs were never compared with measurements from a real system, so under the Q2 rule this is a model run on design data. Moreover, those numbers reflect design optimisation plus solar-profile-matching scheduling versus a commercial Grundfos sizing tool with single-section operation, not the predictive controller itself (the authors note SPM alone accounted for up to 25% of the savings). The actual prototype experiment (seven days, no crops, 0.25 ha simulated field) produced different results: up to 46% higher solar irrigation reliability and a six-fold smaller battery buffer than a simulated SSO reference; it did not measure lifetime cost. The paper states its own limitations (small-scale, seven days, no agronomy validation, 'further work and validation should be conducted to show how the economic results change for different conditions'), but since Q2 is 'no' these are not credited.

notes: Full text appears complete (main text, appendices, references). Study is primary in the sense of own simulation and prototype experiment, but the specific figures in the claim derive from an unvalidated design-stage simulation rather than from measurements of the predictive controller.
